title: Legal careers: Mobility coexists with sector barriers
desc: Links career allocation and rewards to credentials and social background while distinguishing satisfaction, retention and earnings.

kps.k: Frequent job changes can coexist with durable barriers between legal career sectors.
kps.d: Chicago Lawyers distinguishes employer changes from movement between practice categories: 54% of 559 lawyers occupied their starting category at the survey endpoint, including 78% of large-firm starters. This does not establish continuous retention or count promotions and within-category moves. After the JD III likewise finds that few solo or small-firm starters enter larger firms, while larger-firm experience is associated with later in-house employment. Together, these findings characterise mobility as structured by entry position, rather than unrestricted movement through a single career market.

qs.q: At the other extreme, only a third of those who started with govern- ment agencies still worked for a government agency at the time of our survey.“ Overall, 54 percent of the 559 lawyers included in Pan- el A stayed in the category of practice with which they started (however many job changes may have occurred within the category).
qs.a: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar · Academia · 1982

qs.q: For example, very few lawyers who start in solo or small firm practice move into larger private firms, however, some do move into state government positions.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Career-stage turnover and movement away from firms qualify any simple account of sectoral stability.
kps.d: After the JD III follows lawyers who passed a bar in 2000. Its mobility chapter reports job changes falling from 62% during 2003–2007 to 36% during 2007–2013; the overview gives the earlier figure as 63%. Private-firm employment fell from about 70% initially to 48.5% at Wave 3, with business the most frequent destination for firm leavers. These national cohort findings differ from Chicago Lawyers’ emphasis on large-firm category retention, but differing periods, classifications and designs prevent a direct contradiction or a unified historical trend. Leaving a firm, leaving legal practice and leaving paid employment remain distinct outcomes.

qs.q: In Wave 2, 62% of lawyers had changed jobs at least once between 2003 and 2007.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

qs.q: By contrast, as Table 7.1a shows, between 2007 and 2013, 36% of lawyers changed jobs at least once.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Social background and educational credentials correlate with unequal career allocation and rewards.
kps.d: Chicago Lawyers describes socially differentiated career systems centred on corporate-serving large firms and solo practices serving individuals and small businesses. It finds persistent Jewish underrepresentation in large firms across age cohorts, but cannot separate discrimination from self-selection, family traditions or anticipatory avoidance of rejection. After the JD III documents different racial and ethnic sectoral trajectories, a widening gender earnings gap and greater male access to equity partnership. Its largest-firm full-time median incomes were $191,000 for women and $290,000 for men. School prestige and grades also correlate with lucrative placements. These descriptive associations establish disparities, not their causal weights.

qs.q: Lawyers in these different sorts of careers are recruited from systematically varying ethnoreligious and socioeco- nomic origins, and they are trained in different strata of law schools.
qs.a: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar · Academia · 1982

qs.q: In fact, we see that men were more likely to have been promoted to partner and were more likely to have become equity partners than women at the same stage.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Partnership selection, client access and accumulated experience offer possible mechanisms, not established causal explanations.
kps.d: Chicago Lawyers proposes that unsuccessful partnership candidates move to smaller firms and may regain corporate clients after acquiring seniority. It treats initial job stability as a proxy for opportunities to learn and build relationships, not as a direct measure of success. After the JD III tentatively links large-firm departures to partnership timing and economic conditions, and recession resilience to experience, skills, clients and connections. Resilience was uneven: 24% reported reduced compensation and 12% compulsory job changes. The practical implication is to examine training continuity, promotion decisions and subsequent destinations together rather than treating every departure as career failure.

qs.q: Those associates who are not promoted at this point (after five to seven years with a firm) typically will seek placement in smaller and perhaps less prestigious firms where they may be made a partner after a short trial period, thus accounting for the second upward surge.”*
qs.a: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar · Academia · 1982

qs.q: 2 As might be expected given both the economic context and respondents’ career stages (with most respondents in law firms facing the partnership decision after the AJD2 survey), the proportion of AJD lawyers in large law firms (> 250) showed the greatest decline since AJD respondents had begun their careers, from a high of about 18 percent at Wave 1 to 8.3% at Wave 3.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

kps.k: High career satisfaction complicates the use of retention, earnings or job-search intentions as standalone measures of success.
kps.d: After the JD III finds that 76% remained moderately or extremely satisfied with becoming lawyers, despite unequal earnings and promotion. Public-service settings recorded particularly high career satisfaction; large-firm lawyers combined relatively favourable compensation and advancement assessments with low job-setting satisfaction. The report itself uses competing interpretations: its gender chapter assumes active job seekers are most dissatisfied, while its race chapter warns that mobility intentions do not straightforwardly measure dissatisfaction with becoming a lawyer. Career assessment therefore needs to distinguish occupational commitment from satisfaction with a particular employer, pay or working conditions.

qs.q: Twelve years into their careers, 76% of the  16  After the JD III: Third Results of a National Study of Legal Careers  6(&7,21^C^T  respondents report that they are moderately or extremely satisfied with their decision to become a lawyer, a proportion virtually unchanged from prior waves of the survey.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

qs.q: As in the previous reports, the lowest job setting satisfaction was expressed by respondents in the large law firms, led by firms of 101–250 lawyers, followed closely by respondents in the largest law firms.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Measurement and sample design limit claims about changing career barriers and representative professional experience.
kps.d: Chicago Lawyers’ 1975 endpoint confounds age, cohort and organisational change, leaving increasing sector rigidity a hypothesis. After the JD III usually compares each wave’s respondents rather than an identical panel; its supplied accounts also leave setting-exit estimates unreconciled across chapters. Building a Better Bar contributes methodological context, not competence findings: it combines supervisors and juniors, counts 217 employment settings for 201 lawyers, and compares only bar-required jobs with the relevant NALP cohort. Its external demographic figures do not establish its own sample composition. Larger samples, longer follow-up, matched comparisons and explicit denominators would help distinguish career change from compositional change.

qs.q: The presence of si- multaneous changes in the organization of the delivery of legal ser- vices, cohort effects, and age effects therefore make the interpreta- tion of relative changes in retention rates highly problematic.
qs.a: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar · Academia · 1982

qs.q: Thus, some of the differences across waves reflect the fact that a different set of respondents participated in the three waves of the study.
qs.a: After the JD III: Third Results from a National Study of Legal Careers · Academia · 2014

vlens.an: This curated access-to-justice and civil-society source does not take a substantive position on the proposition that legal-career mobility coexists with durable sector barriers shaped by credentials and social background. Its contribution is methodological: it explains that employment-setting counts can exceed the number of lawyers because some participants worked in multiple settings, and that the external comparison was limited to bar-required jobs to align with the study population. These qualifications are relevant to careful measurement of career settings, but the source does not analyse cross-sector mobility, retention, earnings, promotion, educational credentials or social-background disparities. With only this source in the supplied professional voice, there is no evidence from which to identify meaningful internal variation.

qs.q: Sixteen of the junior lawyers in our study worked in two different settings during their first year of practice, so the total number of employment settings is 217 rather than 201.
qs.a: Building a Better Bar: The Twelve Building Blocks of Minimum Competence · Access to justice · 2020

qs.q: Columns four and five contrast those numbers with data reported by the National Association for Law Placement (NALP) for the class of 2017, the modal year in which our junior lawyers earned their law degrees.76 We filtered the NALP data to include only jobs that required bar admission, because our study included only lawyers with jobs that required a license.77

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources accept the proposition that substantial job mobility can coexist with durable barriers between legal career sectors, and they materially develop it through distinct empirical designs. Chicago Lawyers supplies the foundational distinction between changing employers and changing practice-status categories, linking sectoral allocation to social origins and law-school strata. After the JD III extends that account with longitudinal cohort evidence showing that starting settings shape later destinations, even as lawyers move away from private firms and job mobility slows by midcareer. It also broadens the proposition by documenting unequal earnings and promotion, especially by gender, and by separating career satisfaction from retention, pay and job-search intentions. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than overall direction: Chicago Lawyers stresses sectoral persistence and socially differentiated career systems, whereas After the JD III gives greater weight to career-stage turnover, firm exits, movement into business and high satisfaction despite inequality. Both are cautious about causal inference: proposed mechanisms such as partnership selection, discrimination, economic conditions and accumulated experience remain interpretations, while cohort, sampling and measurement differences limit claims about historical change or the profession as a whole.

qs.q: On its face, this may appear to be inconsistent with the hypothesis of increasing rigidity of career lines among the younger cohort, but when the data presented in figure 6.3 is considered in the light of that in table 6.5, it seems that though the younger cohort may change jobs more often, they do not change status categories.
qs.a: Chicago Lawyers: The Social Structure of the Bar · Academia · 1982

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundations accept the proposition that substantial job mobility can coexist with durable barriers between legal career sectors and materially develop it through complementary designs. Chicago Lawyers distinguishes employer turnover from movement across practice-status categories, finding that lawyers may change jobs while remaining within the same sector; it also links sector allocation to social origins and law-school strata. After the JD III adds longitudinal cohort evidence that starting positions shape later destinations, including restricted movement from solo or small-firm practice into larger firms and preferential routes from larger firms into in-house counsel roles. It further broadens the proposition by documenting movement away from private firms, persistent gender and racial inequalities in promotion and earnings, and the need to distinguish career satisfaction from retention, pay and job-search intentions. Material internal variation concerns period, population and measurement rather than the proposition’s core: Chicago Lawyers emphasizes category persistence in a historical Chicago sample, whereas After the JD III records substantial national-cohort movement away from firms by midcareer. Neither design establishes a unified historical trend or the causal weight of mechanisms such as discrimination, self-selection, partnership selection, economic conditions or accumulated experience.

qs.q: On its face, this may appear to be inconsistent with the hypothesis of increasing rigidity of career lines among the younger cohort, but when the data presented in figure 6.3 is considered in the light of that in table 6.5, it seems that though the younger cohort may change jobs more often, they do not change status categories.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source neither supports nor challenges the proposition that job mobility coexists with durable sector barriers shaped by credentials and social background. Its contribution is methodological: it explains that first-year employment-setting counts include supervisors as well as junior lawyers, that some junior lawyers contributed two settings, and that the external comparison was limited to bar-required jobs. These qualifications are relevant to the proposition’s measurement caveat because they show that setting counts and comparison populations require careful interpretation. However, the source provides no evidence about movement between legal sectors, retention, earnings, partnership, educational prestige or social-background disparities. Its demographic references contextualise external studies rather than establishing its own sample’s composition. Accordingly, the evidence is insufficient to determine a substantive position; internal variation is limited to different kinds of methodological qualification rather than competing views on the proposition.
